summary: A proposal by Jon Postel that willing hosts run a Discard process for debugging and measurement. It listens for a connection, completes the Initial Connection Protocol, and throws away every piece of data it receives right away. The connection ends when it is closed.

plainLanguage.summary: A Discard process accepts a network connection and throws away every piece of data it receives. The author suggests it as a simple aid for debugging and measurement.

subtitle: A voluntary Discard process for network debugging and measurement.

tldr.problem: The author proposes a simple service that could help with network debugging and measurement.
tldr.mechanism: A willing host listens for a connection, performs the Initial Connection Protocol, and immediately discards data it receives until the connection closes.
tldr.outcome: The proposal is voluntary and applies only to hosts that choose to implement the Discard process.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 348 as Unknown, with no RFC recorded as updating or obsoleting it. The RFC is a voluntary service proposal.

sections.title: The Discard Proposal
sections.content: Jon Postel suggests that hosts willing to do so implement a Discard process for debugging and measurement. The RFC does not require every host to provide it.
sections.plainLanguage: The author proposes an optional service for network tests. A host can choose whether to run it.

sections.title: Accepting and Discarding Data
sections.content:
The process listens for a connection request and performs the Initial Connection Protocol described in the Current Network Protocols notebook. After the ICP finishes, it waits for data from the Network.

Whenever data arrives, the process discards it at once and reallocates the buffer space. The process ends when the network connections are closed.
sections.plainLanguage: The service establishes a connection in the usual way, then throws away incoming data. It stays active until the connection closes.

sections.title: Scope of the Suggestion
sections.content: The RFC gives a short description of the process and its intended uses. It does not specify a return message or another service beyond receiving and discarding data.
sections.plainLanguage: The process has one job: accept data and discard it. The RFC does not define extra behavior.
